name: Belly Down Armbar from Armbar Control
description: Master the belly down armbar finish from armbar control in BJJ. Learn prone finishing mechanics, grip transitions, and high-percentage completion.
target_area: Elbow joint hyperextension and ulnar collateral ligament
summary: The belly down armbar from armbar control is a prone armbar finish where the attacker rotates face-down over the isolated arm, driving bodyweight and gravity through the elbow to defeat the clasped-hand and stacking defenses that stop the standard supine finish.
overview:
The belly down armbar finish from armbar control is a high-percentage submission completion technique where the attacker transitions from the standard supine armbar position to a prone finishing position. This rotation fundamentally changes the finishing mechanics by channeling the attacker's entire body weight downward through the controlled arm while gravity assists the extension, creating substantially more pressure than the standard hip-bridge finish.

When the defender successfully resists the conventional armbar through clasped hands, stacking, or the hitchhiker escape, the belly-down transition exploits a critical defensive gap. Most armbar defenses are designed for the supine position and become ineffective once the attacker achieves prone orientation. The defender's clasped hands, which provide substantial resistance against upward hip extension, offer minimal protection against the downward crushing pressure of the belly-down position.

From armbar control specifically, this finish is particularly accessible because the attacker already has established grip control, hip proximity, and leg positioning. The transition requires only rotational movement rather than a complete positional change. Competition grapplers frequently chain the standard armbar attempt with the belly-down transition, creating a two-phase attack that forces the defender to address fundamentally different finishing vectors in rapid succession.

injury_risks.injury: Elbow hyperextension with ligament damage to the ulnar collateral ligament
Elbow joint capsule sprain or partial tear from forced extension
Biceps tendon strain or partial tear from resisting extension under load
Distal humerus stress fracture from sustained pressure against locked elbow

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive. The belly down position creates significant mechanical advantage that can damage the elbow extremely quickly. Apply extension gradually and allow adequate time for the tap. Never jerk or spike the arm. The prone position amplifies force beyond what most practitioners expect.
tap_signals: Verbal tap saying 'tap' or any distress vocalization
Physical hand tap on partner, mat, or own body
Physical foot tap on mat with either leg
Any screaming, grunting, or unusual vocalization indicating distress
release_protocol: Release immediately upon any tap signal without waiting for confirmation or repetition
If in doubt whether a tap occurred, release immediately - the position can be re-established safely
Release extension pressure first by lowering the wrist, then release knee squeeze, then disengage completely
Monitor training partner's arm mobility after release and check for signs of injury before continuing
training_restrictions: Beginners should practice mechanics at 50% pressure maximum until transition control is consistent
Always apply extension slowly in training - never jerk or spike the arm during the belly down finish
Do not apply this technique on training partners with known elbow injuries or recent arm submissions
Practice the transition rotation separately from the finishing pressure until both components are reliable

variations_and_setups.description: From supine armbar control, post your far foot on the mat and swing your near leg over the opponent's face while rotating your entire body prone over the controlled arm. This is the highest-percentage entry when the opponent is clasping hands or attempting to stack.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the opponent clasps hands together or stacks forward to defend the standard supine armbar finish

variations_and_setups.description: When the opponent attempts to escape by rolling toward the trapped arm side, follow their momentum and continue the rotation until you achieve the belly-down position on the opposite side. The opponent's own escape attempt provides the rotational energy for the transition.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the opponent initiates a roll or bridge toward the controlled arm to escape the standard armbar

attacker.name: Belly Down Armbar from Armbar Control Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack with the belly down armbar finish from armbar control. Prone finishing mechanics, grip transitions, and defeating common defenses.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the belly down armbar finish from armbar control requires recognizing when standard finishing attempts are being successfully defended and transitioning smoothly to the prone position. The key to this technique is maintaining constant arm isolation throughout the rotational transition while positioning your body weight directly over the controlled elbow joint. The belly-down position transforms the finishing mechanics from a hip-bridge extension to a gravity-assisted compression, creating substantially more pressure with less energy expenditure. Mastery of this transition gives you a reliable answer to the most common armbar defenses and dramatically increases your overall armbar finishing rate from control positions.
key_principles: Maintain constant two-on-one wrist control throughout the entire rotational transition to prevent arm retraction during the vulnerable transition window
Commit fully to the rotation once initiated - hesitation mid-transition creates space for the defender to extract the arm or recover guard
Position the elbow joint directly against your hip crease in the prone position to create the optimal fulcrum for extension pressure
Use gravity and body weight as the primary finishing force rather than arm strength - the prone position makes this natural
Keep knees pinched tightly together around the controlled arm to eliminate lateral escape angles and maintain arm isolation
Apply extension progressively and slowly - the mechanical advantage in belly-down is enormous and can cause injury faster than expected
setup_requirements: Established armbar control with both hands securing the opponent's wrist or forearm in a grip that will survive rotation
Hips positioned close to the opponent's shoulder with perpendicular body alignment creating the initial armbar threat
Recognition that the standard supine finish is being effectively defended through clasped hands, stacking, or rotational escape
At least one foot posted on the mat to provide the push-off point for initiating the rotational transition

execution_steps.action: Recognize defense and commit to transition
execution_steps.description: Identify when the standard armbar finish is being successfully defended through hand clasping, stacking, or rotational defense. Make the deliberate decision to transition to belly-down rather than continuing to fight for the supine finish, which wastes energy against effective defense.
execution_steps.timing: Immediate recognition within 2-3 seconds of failed standard finish attempt

execution_steps.description: Adjust both hands onto the opponent's wrist with a strong monkey grip or two-on-one configuration where thumbs wrap fully around the wrist. This grip must survive the rotational transition, so squeeze forearms together to create a vise that prevents any slack during movement.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds to secure grip before initiating rotation

execution_steps.action: Post far foot and initiate rotation
execution_steps.description: Plant your far foot firmly on the mat and begin swinging your near leg over the opponent's face and body in an arc. Simultaneously pull the controlled wrist tight to your chest while driving off your posted foot. Maintain constant tension on the arm throughout this movement to prevent retraction.
execution_steps.timing: Explosive initiation, 1 second to begin the swing

execution_steps.action: Complete the prone rotation over the arm
execution_steps.description: Continue rotating your entire body over the controlled arm until you are face-down on the mat. Your chest should press against the back of their forearm with their elbow joint positioned directly against your hip crease. Keep the wrist pulled tight throughout the full rotation arc.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds to complete the full rotation to prone position

execution_steps.description: Once prone, immediately pinch your knees together around the opponent's upper arm, press your hips heavily into the mat, and tuck the controlled wrist tight against your sternum. Your body weight should drive directly downward through the arm, eliminating all space between your body and their limb.
execution_steps.timing: Immediate stabilization upon reaching prone position

execution_steps.action: Apply gradual extension for the finish
execution_steps.description: Arch your lower back gently while curling their wrist toward your chest, creating a slow lever action across the elbow joint. Apply pressure progressively and monitor for tap signals throughout. The mechanical advantage in this position is enormous, so minimal force generates significant joint stress.
execution_steps.timing: Slow progressive application over 3-5 seconds, never jerking or spiking

execution_steps.action: Monitor for tap and maintain control
execution_steps.description: Stay alert for all tap signals including verbal, hand tap, and foot tap while maintaining your control position. Keep knees squeezed and hips heavy. If the opponent attempts to bridge or roll, follow their movement while maintaining arm isolation rather than fighting their momentum.
execution_steps.timing: Continuous awareness throughout the entire finishing sequence

common_counters.counter: Opponent clasps hands together during the rotation to prevent arm isolation
common_counters.your_response: Wedge your forearm between their clasped hands as a lever, or switch to attacking the top hand grip by peeling fingers. You can also complete the rotation and use the belly-down body weight to break the grip from prone.

common_counters.counter: Opponent turns into you and attempts to sit up during the transition
common_counters.your_response: Accelerate the rotation to complete the prone position before they can fully sit up. If they achieve a partial sit-up, use your leg across their face to push them back down while completing the transition.

common_counters.counter: Opponent bridges explosively and attempts to pull arm free during the rotation window
common_counters.your_response: Tighten your two-on-one wrist grip and absorb the bridge momentum by following their hip movement. Use their bridge energy to assist your rotation rather than fighting it. Pinch knees immediately upon reaching prone.

common_counters.counter: Opponent shrimps away and recovers closed guard during the transition
common_counters.your_response: If you feel the arm slipping, immediately abandon the belly-down attempt and return to standard armbar control. Re-establish hip proximity and leg control before attempting the transition again or switching to triangle.

common_errors.error: Releasing wrist control during the rotation to post a hand on the mat
common_errors.consequence: The opponent retracts their arm during the grip-free moment, escaping the submission entirely and potentially recovering to closed guard or half guard
common_errors.correction: Maintain two-on-one wrist control throughout the entire rotation. Use your posted foot and core rotation to drive the transition rather than relying on a hand post for balance.

common_errors.error: Rotating too slowly and allowing the opponent to follow and recover guard
common_errors.consequence: The opponent tracks your rotation, hip escapes underneath, and recovers to closed guard, negating the armbar control position entirely
common_errors.correction: Commit to the rotation with decisive speed once initiated. The transition should be one fluid explosive movement, not a cautious incremental rotation that gives the defender time to react.

common_errors.error: Landing with hips too far from the opponent's shoulder in the prone position
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient leverage for the finish because the fulcrum point is displaced from the elbow joint, requiring excessive arm strength to generate extension pressure
common_errors.correction: During the rotation, actively scoot your hips toward the opponent's shoulder. In the final prone position, their elbow should sit directly in your hip crease with zero gap between your body and their shoulder.

common_errors.error: Failing to pinch knees together after completing the prone rotation
common_errors.consequence: The opponent can rotate their arm laterally and slip the elbow free, or use the space to turn their body and begin recovering position
common_errors.correction: Immediately squeeze your knees together around the opponent's upper arm upon reaching the prone position. The knee pinch is the primary control mechanism that prevents arm extraction in belly-down.

common_errors.error: Applying extension too rapidly or jerking the arm in the belly-down position
common_errors.consequence: Serious elbow injury to the training partner because the mechanical advantage in prone position amplifies force dramatically, and the defender has limited time to signal a tap
common_errors.correction: Always apply extension slowly and progressively in belly-down. The position generates far more force than the standard armbar, so treat the finishing pressure with extra caution and allow ample time for tap recognition.

common_errors.error: Keeping legs straight and flat on the mat instead of curling heels toward the hips
common_errors.consequence: Reduced control over the opponent's arm and body, allowing them to bridge and create space or roll out of the submission attempt
common_errors.correction: Curl your heels toward your glutes to create active downward pressure through your thighs and knees. This leg position maximizes the clamping force around the arm and keeps your weight concentrated over the elbow joint.

training_progressions.focus: Learning the basic rotational movement from supine to prone
training_progressions.description: Practice the rotation with a cooperative partner who holds their arm in place. Focus on maintaining wrist control throughout the full rotation arc, proper foot posting, and landing with hips tight to the shoulder. No finishing pressure applied. Perform 20 repetitions per side.

training_progressions.focus: Maintaining arm isolation during the transition against light resistance
training_progressions.description: Partner provides 30-40% resistance by attempting to retract their arm during the rotation. Practice adjusting grip pressure dynamically while completing the transition. Focus on the moment of highest vulnerability when your body is mid-rotation.

training_progressions.focus: Applying extension safely from the established belly-down position
training_progressions.description: From an already-established belly-down position, practice the finishing mechanics at controlled intensity. Focus on progressive extension through hip positioning and back arch rather than arm pulling. Partner taps early while you develop pressure sensitivity.

training_progressions.focus: Linking the standard armbar attempt to belly-down transition against active defense
training_progressions.description: Start from armbar control, attempt the standard finish, and flow to belly-down when partner defends. Partner uses 60-75% resistance with realistic defense. Practice recognizing the trigger for transition and executing the complete sequence fluidly.

training_progressions.focus: Applying the belly-down finish in live training rounds
training_progressions.description: Begin rounds in armbar control and work to finish via either standard or belly-down armbar. Partner uses full defensive effort. Focus on reading which finish is available based on defensive reactions and transitioning without telegraphing.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structure does the belly down armbar finish primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The belly down armbar primarily attacks the elbow joint by forcing hyperextension against the ulnar collateral ligament and joint capsule. The prone position creates a lever where the hip crease acts as the fulcrum against the posterior elbow, and the downward body weight combined with wrist curl generates extension force that stresses the ligaments preventing the elbow from bending backward.

flashcards.question: Your opponent clasps their hands together as you begin rotating to belly-down - what adjustment prevents the defense from succeeding?
flashcards.answer: Complete the rotation to prone position even with their hands clasped, because the belly-down body weight creates far more grip-breaking force than the supine position. Once prone, wedge your forearm between their clasped hands and lever them apart, or attack the top hand by peeling individual fingers. The gravity-assisted pressure of the prone position makes hand clasping a temporary delay rather than a permanent defense.

plausible: Sit back and wait for fatigue

flashcards.question: What grip configuration must you maintain throughout the rotational transition?
flashcards.answer: Maintain a strong two-on-one wrist grip where both hands wrap around the opponent's wrist with thumbs overlapping on the inside. Forearms should squeeze together creating a vise around the wrist. This grip must never release during the rotation, as any momentary slack allows arm retraction. The monkey grip variation with interlocking fingers around the wrist provides the most secure hold during dynamic movement.

flashcards.question: At what point during the belly down armbar sequence does the defender pass the point of no escape?
flashcards.answer: The point of no escape occurs when the attacker completes the prone rotation with knees pinched and hips tight to the shoulder. Once the attacker's body weight is driving downward through the arm with knees clamped, the defender cannot generate sufficient force to retract the arm or rotate out. The transition window is the last reliable escape opportunity, which is why defenders must act before the rotation completes.

flashcards.question: What is the most common finishing error that reduces belly down armbar effectiveness?
flashcards.answer: The most common error is landing with hips too far from the opponent's shoulder after the rotation. This displaces the fulcrum point from the elbow joint and forces the attacker to rely on arm strength rather than body weight for the finish. The correction is to actively scoot hips toward the shoulder during and after the rotation, ensuring the elbow sits directly in the hip crease with zero gap.
flashcards.answer_line: Hips too far from their shoulder

flashcards.question: Your opponent starts bridging explosively during your belly-down rotation - how do you adjust?
flashcards.answer: Absorb the bridge momentum by following the opponent's hip movement rather than fighting against it. Tighten your wrist grip and use their upward energy to assist your rotation. As they bridge, their arm extends slightly which actually helps your finishing position. Once they return to the mat, immediately pinch knees and establish the prone control. Their bridge energy is wasted against the rotational transition.
flashcards.answer_line: Follow the bridge, keep grip tight

plausible: Drive down to stop the bridge

flashcards.question: Why must extension pressure be applied slowly in the belly-down position compared to the standard armbar?
flashcards.answer: The belly-down position creates dramatically greater mechanical advantage than the standard supine armbar because the attacker's entire body weight drives through the arm via gravity rather than just hip bridge force. This amplified leverage means the elbow reaches its structural limit much faster with less perceived effort from the attacker. Applying pressure quickly risks serious ligament damage or fracture before the defender can signal a tap.

flashcards.question: What is the proper release protocol after your opponent taps to the belly down armbar?
flashcards.answer: Release extension pressure immediately by lowering the wrist away from your chest, then release the knee squeeze around the arm, then disengage completely from the prone position. Do not wait for a second tap or verbal confirmation. Check your partner's elbow mobility and ask about any discomfort before continuing training. If there is any doubt about whether a tap occurred, release immediately since the position can be safely re-established.
flashcards.answer_line: Free the wrist, then the knees

plausible: Let the knees go before the wrist
Keep light control after the tap
trap: Hold the lock for a second tap

flashcards.question: In competition, how do you set up the belly-down transition to maximize finishing probability?
flashcards.answer: In competition, use the standard armbar finish as a genuine first attack rather than a feint. Apply real finishing pressure from supine to force the opponent into committed defensive reactions like hand clasping or stacking. When you feel their defense lock in, immediately transition to belly-down while their defensive structure is oriented against the wrong finishing vector. The two-phase attack is most effective when both threats are real.

flashcards.question: What indicators tell you the elbow is approaching its structural breaking point during the belly-down finish?
flashcards.answer: Key indicators include the arm reaching full extension against resistance, visible straightening of the elbow joint, the defender's body tensing or arching involuntarily, any vocalization or facial expression of distress, and feeling the arm become rigid against your hip pressure. When you feel the arm lock out against your extension pressure with no remaining flexion, the joint is at its structural limit. Ease pressure slightly and wait for the tap rather than continuing to apply force past this point.
flashcards.answer_line: Arm locks out, no give left

trap: Continue until you hear a pop

defender.name: Belly Down Armbar from Armbar Control Defender
defender.description: Defend against the belly down armbar finish from armbar control. Recognition cues, escape timing, and techniques to prevent the prone arm finish.
defender.overview: Defending the belly down armbar from armbar control demands early recognition of the attacker's rotational transition and immediate defensive action during the narrow transition window. Once the attacker achieves the prone finishing position, standard armbar defenses such as the hitchhiker escape, hand clasping, and stacking become mechanically ineffective against the downward crushing pressure. The defender must prioritize preventing the rotation from completing by controlling the attacker's hips, extracting the arm during the transition, or turning into the attacker to deny the prone angle. Understanding the transition timing is critical because the window for effective defense closes rapidly once the rotation begins, making early recognition the single most important defensive skill.
key_principles: Recognize the rotational transition early - the moment the attacker posts their foot and begins swinging their leg is your last high-percentage defensive window
Keep your elbow bent and pulled tight to your body at all times to prevent the attacker from achieving the arm extension needed for the finish
Turn your body toward the attacker during the transition to prevent them from completing the prone rotation over your arm
Use your free hand to control the attacker's hip or far leg, disrupting the rotation mechanics and preventing them from completing the transition
If the belly-down position is established, tap early - the mechanical advantage is enormous and the position deteriorates faster than you expect
Create connection between your trapped arm and your torso by grabbing your own wrist, bicep, or lapel to resist arm isolation
recognition_cues: The attacker posts their far foot on the mat while maintaining wrist control, indicating they are preparing to generate rotational force for the transition
The attacker's near leg begins swinging over your face or head in an arc while they pull your wrist tighter to their chest
You feel a rotational pulling force on your trapped arm combined with the attacker's body weight shifting from beside you to over your arm
The attacker consolidates both hands specifically onto your wrist in a tight monkey grip, abandoning any bicep or forearm control in favor of maximum wrist security

defensive_options.action: Turn into the attacker and sit up during the rotation
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you recognize the leg swing beginning and before the attacker reaches the halfway point of the rotation
defensive_options.if_successful: Prevents the prone position from being established and returns both players to a contested armbar control scramble where standard defenses remain viable
defensive_options.risk: If the attacker is already past the rotation midpoint, turning in may accelerate their transition rather than stopping it

defensive_options.action: Retract arm explosively during the mid-rotation grip vulnerability
defensive_options.when_to_use: During the 1-2 second window when the attacker's body is mid-rotation and their grip is under maximum dynamic stress from the movement
defensive_options.if_successful: Frees the trapped arm entirely and allows immediate guard recovery or scramble to a neutral position
defensive_options.risk: If the grip holds, the failed extraction attempt extends your arm into the finishing position, making the belly-down finish easier

defensive_options.action: Hip escape away and recover closed guard during the transition
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker commits fully to the rotation and you cannot prevent it, use their movement commitment to create space for guard recovery
defensive_options.if_successful: Recovers to closed guard where the armbar threat is neutralized and you have established a safe defensive position
defensive_options.risk: Requires precise timing and sufficient hip mobility; if too slow, you end up in belly-down with your arm extended

escape_paths: Turn into the attacker and sit up before the rotation completes, using your free hand on their hip to block the transition and recover to standard armbar defense position
Explosive arm retraction during the mid-rotation window when the attacker's dynamic movement creates momentary grip vulnerability
Hip escape and guard recovery by shrimping away during the attacker's committed rotation, pulling your arm free as distance increases

favorable_outcomes.how: Prevent the belly-down rotation by sitting up and turning into the attacker during the transition window, forcing them back to standard armbar control where all standard defenses remain available
Extract the trapped arm during the mid-rotation grip vulnerability and immediately recover to closed guard by pulling the attacker into your guard as they lose arm control

common_errors.error: Waiting until the attacker is fully prone before attempting to defend
common_errors.consequence: Once the belly-down position is established with knees pinched and hips heavy, escape probability drops below 15% and the mechanical advantage makes continued defense extremely dangerous for the elbow
common_errors.correction: React during the transition, not after. The moment you feel the rotational cue or see the leg swing, immediately initiate your defensive response. The transition window is your primary escape opportunity.

common_errors.error: Straightening the arm to try to pull it free from the prone position
common_errors.consequence: Extending the arm into the belly-down finish gives the attacker exactly what they need - a straight arm under their body weight creates the optimal finishing position and dramatically increases injury risk
common_errors.correction: Keep the elbow bent at all costs. Pull your wrist toward your own shoulder, clasp your hands together, or grab your own bicep to maintain flexion. Never extend against the prone position.

common_errors.error: Attempting the hitchhiker escape against the belly-down position
common_errors.consequence: The hitchhiker escape relies on rotating the arm under the attacker's hips, but the prone position eliminates the space this escape requires. The attempt wastes energy and time without creating any escape progress.
common_errors.correction: Abandon hitchhiker escape attempts once the attacker achieves prone position. Focus on bridge-and-roll escapes or tap if the arm begins to extend. The hitchhiker only works against the supine armbar.

common_errors.error: Bridging directly upward against the belly-down attacker
common_errors.consequence: Bridging up feeds energy into the attacker's downward pressure system and can actually accelerate the arm extension by lifting the elbow into their hip fulcrum
common_errors.correction: If bridging, bridge laterally toward the trapped arm side to create rotation rather than upward extension. The goal is to turn the attacker off your arm, not to lift them.

flashcards.question: What are the earliest recognition cues that indicate the attacker is transitioning to a belly-down armbar finish?
flashcards.answer: The earliest cues are the attacker posting their far foot on the mat, consolidating both hands specifically onto your wrist in a tight monkey grip, and their near leg beginning to swing over your face in an arc. You may also feel a rotational pulling force on your trapped arm combined with their body weight shifting from beside you to over your arm. Recognizing these cues immediately is critical because the defensive window closes within 1-2 seconds.

plausible: They flatten their back to mat

flashcards.question: When should you tap to the belly down armbar finish rather than continuing to defend?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately when the attacker has established the prone position with knees pinched and hips tight, and your arm begins to straighten against your resistance. The belly-down position amplifies force dramatically beyond the standard armbar, meaning the elbow reaches its structural limit much faster than you expect. If you feel your arm extending despite maximum defensive effort, tap before you feel a pop or sharp pain. There is no technical defense once the arm begins to straighten under prone body weight.
flashcards.answer_line: When your arm starts to straighten

plausible: Once the arm is fully extended
trap: When you feel the elbow pop

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available during the attacker's rotational transition?
flashcards.answer: During the transition, you can turn into the attacker and sit up to prevent the rotation from completing, explosively retract your arm during the mid-rotation grip vulnerability when dynamic movement stresses their grip, or hip escape away to recover closed guard while the attacker is committed to the rotational movement. All three options must be executed during the 1-2 second transition window before prone position is established.
flashcards.answer_line: Sit up, retract arm, or hip escape

plausible: Bridge hard to buck them off

flashcards.question: Why does the hitchhiker escape fail against the belly-down armbar position?
flashcards.answer: The hitchhiker escape works against the standard supine armbar by rotating the arm under the attacker's hips and sliding the elbow across to escape. In the belly-down position, the attacker's entire body weight pins the arm against the mat, eliminating the space required for the rotational escape. The downward pressure vector makes it mechanically impossible to slide the elbow underneath, rendering the hitchhiker completely ineffective against the prone finish.
flashcards.answer_line: Body weight pins arm, no space

plausible: It only works with a gi grip
Needs both hands free to spin
trap: Spin the arm anyway and hold

flashcards.question: How should you bridge when defending against the established belly-down armbar?
flashcards.answer: Bridge laterally toward the trapped arm side rather than directly upward. Bridging up feeds energy into the attacker's downward pressure system and can accelerate arm extension by lifting the elbow into their hip fulcrum. Bridging laterally creates rotation that may shift the attacker off your arm and disrupt their knee pinch. However, if the prone position is fully established with tight control, bridging alone is unlikely to create escape and you should prioritize tapping safely over continued resistance.

plausible: Shrimp your hips away from them
trap: Bridge straight up into their hips

training_progressions.focus: Identifying the transition cues and building defensive reflexes
training_progressions.description: Partner repeatedly sets up and initiates the belly-down transition at slow speed. Defender focuses purely on recognizing the cues: foot post, grip consolidation, and leg swing. Call out each cue verbally as it occurs. No actual defense attempted yet, just recognition training.

training_progressions.focus: Executing defensive actions during the rotational transition
training_progressions.description: Partner performs the belly-down transition at 50% speed. Defender practices all three defensive options in sequence: sit up and turn in, explosive arm retraction, and hip escape to guard. Perform 10 repetitions of each defense, focusing on timing the response to the transition window.

training_progressions.focus: Developing safe tap timing when defense fails
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes the belly-down position and applies very slow extension pressure. Defender practices recognizing when the arm begins to straighten beyond their defensive capacity and tapping before structural stress. This drill builds the judgment to distinguish between defensible and indefensible positions.

training_progressions.focus: Applying all defensive skills against full-speed attacks
training_progressions.description: Start in armbar control with partner using full offensive effort including standard finish attempts and belly-down transitions. Defender uses recognition, transition defense, and tap awareness in combination. Focus on choosing the right defensive response based on the attacker's timing and commitment level.
